passage: The harvest of the community orchard on Pilgrims Hill set a record this autumn, and the surplus has forced a pleasant problem on the volunteers who run it: what to do with eleven tons of apples. The orchard, planted on a former landfill cap in 2011 with 340 trees of 27 heritage varieties, produced roughly double last year's crop, a jump the volunteers attribute to a wet June and to the pruning course that 19 of them completed last winter. The group's cider press, bought secondhand for 1,400 dollars, has run every weekend since September, and the juice, sold at the Saturday market, has raised 6,200 dollars so far, earmarked for a deer fence after saplings on the north edge were browsed bare. Three food charities collect fruit on Thursdays, taking about a ton a week between them. The volunteers have also revived an old custom: any resident may pick freely from the six trees nearest the gate, marked with yellow ribbons. Coordinator Sefa Adjapong said the group will graft cuttings from their best cropper, a russet called Dunmow Pippin, onto 40 new rootstocks in the spring.
question: How many trees were planted in the community orchard in 2011?

passage: Firefighters spent Sunday afternoon rescuing a window cleaner whose platform jammed 110 feet up the side of the Colville insurance building, a slow and methodical operation that closed two streets and drew a patient crowd. The platform, a two man cradle, stopped moving at about 1:30 p.m. when its drive motor failed, leaving the cleaner, who was working alone, suspended between the ninth and tenth floors in a gusting wind. The building's own winch team could not budge the cradle, so the fire service brought its high angle unit, which lowered a rescuer from the roof on twin ropes. The rescuer clipped the cleaner into a harness, and both were lowered to the pavement at 4:05 p.m., to applause. The cleaner, a 44 year old with 20 years in the trade, declined a hospital check and reportedly asked first about his squeegee, which had fallen early in the ordeal and lodged in a third floor lighting cove, where it remained on Monday. The safety office has impounded the cradle; its motor had passed inspection in May. The building's remaining windows, a spokesman confirmed, will be cleaned by a different method.
question: At what time were the cleaner and rescuer lowered to the pavement?

passage: The village of Trelow has won its long argument with the mapping agency: the agency confirmed this week that the next edition of the regional sheet will mark the hill above the village as Trelow Beacon, the name every local generation has used, rather than Mount Hobbs, the name printed on maps since 1907. The error, the parish council argued in a dossier submitted two years ago, began with a surveyor who mistook the name of a landowner, one J. Hobbs, recorded in a field book, for the name of the hill itself. The council's case rested on tithe records from 1841, a chapel banner embroidered in 1876, and the minutes of the beacon bonfire committee, which has organized fires on the summit for royal occasions since 1897 without once calling the hill anything but the Beacon. The agency's naming panel, which considers about 30 such cases a year and grants perhaps a third of them, called the evidence unusually complete. The new sheet prints in the spring. The landlord of the village inn, which has sold a Mount Hobbs bitter since the 1990s, says the beer will be renamed too, once the current pump clips wear out.
question: What name will the next edition of the map give the hill?

passage: A dispute over a prize pumpkin has ended in a shared trophy at the Ferris Vale autumn show, after judges discovered that the two heaviest entries, weighed at 611 pounds and 608 pounds, had grown from seeds of the same fruit and been raised by brothers who have not spoken in six years. The heavier pumpkin belonged to Aldric Vane, the lighter to his younger brother Corwin, and the three pound margin fell within the tolerance of the show's aging scale, which the rules say must decide only when the gap exceeds five pounds. The head judge, citing that rule, declared a tie, the first in the show's 74 years. The brothers, who grew up showing vegetables with their father, a twelve time champion, shook hands at the presentation, and were later seen comparing notes on fertilizer by the beer tent, a development the show secretary called the real prize. The winning seeds trace back to a 590 pound fruit their father showed in 2009. Between them the brothers also took first in leeks and second in gooseberries. The show drew 3,100 visitors, its best gate since the rain year of 2017, and raised 8,400 dollars for the district nursing fund.
question: How much did the heavier of the two pumpkins weigh?

passage: The last public telephone box in the county will be preserved as a listed structure, the heritage office ruled on Thursday, ending a removal order that had been posted on its door since June. The box, on the green at Nether Soley, was installed in 1936 and is one of the cast iron type with the domed roof, of which fewer than 40 survive in the region. The phone itself was disconnected in 2021 after logging, the operator said, just eleven calls in its final year, four of them to the speaking clock. The parish council fought removal not for the phone but for the box, which doubles as the village's book exchange, seed library in spring, and, by long custom, the place where the flower show entry forms are posted. The listing requires the operator to leave the box in place and keep its exterior painted; the council takes over the glazing and the light, which it will convert to solar. A celebration is planned at which the oldest resident, who remembers the box being installed when she was nine, will make a ceremonial call from a donated handset wired to a speaker, since the line itself will not return.
question: In what year was the telephone box at Nether Soley installed?

passage: Rail passengers between Loxton and the ferry port faced a fourth consecutive morning of delays on Friday, and the operator has now published the cause: a signal cable gnawed through in three places by beavers that have dammed the drainage ditch beside the line at Marsh Colne. The animals, whose lodge now stands within twenty feet of the track bed, severed the cable first on Tuesday, and two temporary splices have each failed in turn as the family continued working the ditch. Trains are running under manual signaling through the section, adding about 25 minutes to the 70 minute journey. The operator cannot simply remove the dam: beavers are protected, and the wildlife agency must license any interference with an active lodge. A joint inspection on Thursday agreed on a plan to reroute the cable overhead on poles for 400 yards, work promised within ten days, and to install a flow device that lowers the pond gradually without alarming the animals. A wildlife agency officer noted the beavers had chosen the wettest cutting on the line and called the site, from their point of view, excellent. The operator declined to estimate the week's cost, saying only that it exceeded the price of the poles.
question: What animals damaged the signal cable at Marsh Colne?

passage: A violin left on the number 14 tram in March has been reunited with its owner after a search that involved three countries, a pawnshop ledger, and the sharp memory of a depot cleaner. The instrument, made in 1907 and valued at about 60,000 dollars, belongs to the touring soloist Elka Marovic, who realized it was missing only when the tram had already returned to the depot. The case first went unnoticed in lost property, logged simply as luggage, black. A cleaner, Dov Berkovich, recalled setting it in the office himself, but by the time Marovic's manager called, the case had been claimed in error by a music student who had lost a nearly identical one the same week. The student, discovering the mistake, had tried to return it to the tram office, found it closed for a holiday, and left for a semester abroad with the violin in her mother's flat. The trail was untangled when the student pawned her own recovered case, of all things, and the pawnbroker's ledger note about a mixup reached a collectors forum. Marovic collected the violin on Tuesday, played a short thank you concert in the depot canteen on Wednesday, and has endowed a small annual bonus for the lost property office.
question: Who is the owner of the violin left on the tram?

passage: The town council of Brindle Heath voted on Tuesday to buy the failing indoor market hall for 1 dollar, taking on with it a repair bill estimated at 2.6 million dollars and a roster of 19 remaining traders, down from 70 in the hall's best years. The seller, a property fund that acquired the hall in 2015, had sought planning consent to demolish it for flats and was refused twice, the building being a rare survivor of the 1904 iron and glass type. Under the deal the fund also pays the council 400,000 dollars toward the roof, whose failing glazing bars are the most urgent item. The council's plan, drawn with the traders association, phases repairs over four years while keeping the hall open, moves traders to the sound eastern aisle first, and reserves six stalls at reduced rent for food startups. A cafe operator has signed for the corner unit with the clock, promising to restore the clock itself, stopped at ten past four since anyone can remember. Council leader Petra Osei called the purchase a calculated risk and noted the hall sits between the two busiest bus stops in town, with 11,000 boardings a week between them.
question: For how much did the council buy the market hall?

passage: An amateur meteor hunter has recovered fragments of the fireball that lit up the coast on the night of the 12th, guided by doorbell cameras, a fisherman's dashcam, and arithmetic done at his kitchen table. Physics teacher Osman Adeel triangulated the fall using timestamps from nine video clips volunteered through a community page he set up the morning after the event, narrowing the likely strewn field to a band of pasture two miles long behind the dunes at Welk. On his third day of searching, and after two false alarms involving sea coal, he found a fusion crusted stone of 140 grams beside a fence post, and within a week organized searches by 60 volunteers in line abreast had turned up eight more pieces, the largest at 410 grams, for a total just over a kilogram. The fragments, provisionally classed as an ordinary chondrite, are being examined at the provincial institute, which will keep 20 percent by weight under the standard arrangement while the rest returns to the finders and landowners. Adeel has asked that the main stone go on loan to his school. The last recovered fall in the province was in 1962.
question: How much does the largest recovered fragment weigh?

passage: The bells of St. Anselm's rang a full peal on Saturday for the first time in 31 years, three hours and 22 minutes of continuous ringing that marked the end of a restoration which saw all eight bells lowered, retuned, and rehung on a new steel frame. The oldest bell, cast in 1671 and known as Old Gabriel, cracked in 1994, silencing full circle ringing ever since; it has now been welded, a repair the founders guaranteed for a century, and returned as the tenor. The work cost 310,000 dollars, raised over six years through a trust, two legacies, and an open tower day that let 1,900 visitors climb to the frame. The peal itself, a composition of 5,040 changes, was rung by a visiting band of eight after the home ringers, by their own cheerful admission, judged themselves not yet match fit; the local band of eleven, five of them recruits trained during the restoration on a simulator, rang a shorter touch at evensong. A peal board recording the names will be painted for the ringing chamber. The vicar noted one unforeseen effect: the retuned bells are audible in Fenn End, a mile further than before, and the first complaint arrived by Sunday.
question: What is the name of the oldest bell?
